newsitem.title: USA: California school board recognizes 'Black English'.
newsitem.headline: California school board recognizes 'Black English'.

text.p: A California school board has adopted a policy recognising so-called Ebonics, or Black English, as a primary language for many of its black students, school officials said on Thursday.

The resolution, approved by the Oakland, Calif., school board on Wednesday night, calls on the district to provide teacher training in Ebonics, recognise it as distinct from standard English and help black students who use Ebonics to master standard English.

"It's not just bad English," Oakland Unified School District spokeswoman Sherri Willis said of Ebonics. "Rather than call it subpar, we're acknowledging their language skills with the goal in mind to help them master reading, writing and speaking standard English."

Willis said district educators hope the programme -- which may be the first in the nation -- will help improve the performance of black students in school. An estimated 53 percent of Oakland's nearly 52,000 students are black and officials said they have the lowest average grade point averages in the district.

District officials said linguists recognise Ebonics as a distinct language with origins in the West and Niger-Congo African languages. It has distinct syntax patterns and grammar, such as the absence of the forms of the verb "to be."

"Whatever we are using now is not working. In my day, they would teach you how to talk like the white folks," school board member Toni Cook told the San Francisco Chronicle. "Because someone says, 'I be,' does not mean someone is intellectually deficient."
California state education officials declined to comment on the policy, saying they planned to review the Oakland resolution in the coming days.

The resolution requires the district to officially recognise "the existence and the cultural and historic bases of West and Niger-Congo African language systems, and each language as the predominantly primary language of African-American students."

It also requires that the district implement an academic programme to teach black students "in their primary language for the combined purposes of maintaining the legitimacy and richness of (Ebonics) and to facilitate their acquisition and mastery of English language skills."
Willis said it was not clear how the district would fund the programme. District officials said they may try to obtain federal funds for billingual education programmes.
